body_es:
En Domain-Driven Design, los objetos del dominio se clasifican en dos tipos principales según su naturaleza de identidad.

Una entidad (Entity) es un objeto con identidad propia que persiste en el tiempo. Dos entidades con los mismos atributos son objetos distintos si tienen IDs diferentes. Un usuario, un pedido o una cuenta bancaria son entidades: lo que importa no es el valor de sus atributos sino quiénes son (su identidad). Las entidades son mutables: su estado cambia a lo largo de su ciclo de vida.

Un objeto de valor (Value Object) es un objeto definido exclusivamente por sus atributos. No tiene identidad propia: dos objetos de valor con los mismos atributos son intercambiables e iguales. El dinero, las coordenadas geográficas, un rango de fechas o una dirección postal son objetos de valor. Los value objects deben ser inmutables: en lugar de modificarlos, se reemplazan por nuevas instancias.

Usar value objects correctamente reduce la complejidad: como son inmutables, son thread-safe por definición, se pueden compartir sin riesgo y simplifican las comparaciones de igualdad. En Python, los dataclasses con `frozen=True` o las namedtuples son implementaciones naturales de value objects.
body_en:
In Domain-Driven Design, domain objects are classified by their identity semantics into two types.

An Entity is an object with its own persistent identity. Two entities with identical attribute values are still distinct objects if their IDs differ. A user, an order, or a bank account is an entity—what matters is not what it currently looks like but who it is. Entities are mutable: their attributes change over their lifecycle, but their identity does not.

A Value Object is defined entirely by its attributes. It has no identity of its own: two value objects with the same attribute values are equal and interchangeable. Money, GPS coordinates, a date range, or a mailing address are value objects. Value objects must be immutable: instead of mutating one, you create a new instance with the changed value.

Immutability makes value objects inherently thread-safe, safe to share, and trivial to compare. In Python, `dataclass(frozen=True)` or `NamedTuple` are natural implementations. The example shows both types and demonstrates their different equality semantics.
example_code:
from dataclasses import dataclass

# Entity — identity is the id field, not the attributes
class User:
    def __init__(self, user_id, name, email):
        self.user_id = user_id
        self.name = name
        self.email = email

    def __eq__(self, other):
        return isinstance(other, User) and self.user_id == other.user_id

    def __repr__(self):
        return f'User(id={self.user_id}, name={self.name!r})'

# Value Object — identity IS the attributes; immutable
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Money:
    amount: int   # in cents to avoid float issues
    currency: str

    def __repr__(self):
        return f'Money({self.amount / 100:.2f} {self.currency})'

u1 = User('u-1', 'Alice', 'alice@example.com')
u2 = User('u-1', 'Alice', 'alice@CHANGED.com')
u3 = User('u-2', 'Alice', 'alice@example.com')

print(f'u1 == u2 (same id, different email): {u1 == u2}')
print(f'u1 == u3 (different id, same name):  {u1 == u3}')

m1 = Money(1099, 'USD')
m2 = Money(1099, 'USD')
m3 = Money(1099, 'EUR')
print(f'm1 == m2 (same amount, same currency): {m1 == m2}')
print(f'm1 == m3 (same amount, diff currency): {m1 == m3}')
example_output:
u1 == u2 (same id, different email): True
u1 == u3 (different id, same name):  False
m1 == m2 (same amount, same currency): True
m1 == m3 (same amount, diff currency): False
source: Evans, E. — Domain-Driven Design (Addison-Wesley, 2003) ch. 5 — https://www.domainlanguage.com/ddd/
